text_blocks.snippet: Most people experience flu-like symptoms within 2 to 4 weeks after contracting HIV. These symptoms, which can include fever, headache, and rash, may last for a few days or several weeks. However, some people have no symptoms at all, and the only way to know for sure if you have HIV is to get tested.

list.title: Acute HIV Infection:
list.snippet: This early stage, also known as primary infection, typically occurs 2 to 4 weeks after infection. During this period, the virus replicates rapidly, and some individuals experience flu-like symptoms.

list.title: Chronic HIV Infection:
list.snippet: After the acute phase, HIV can progress to a chronic, or asymptomatic, stage where the virus continues to multiply but at lower levels. Many people don't experience any noticeable symptoms during this stage.

list.title: AIDS:
list.snippet: If HIV is left untreated, it can progress to AIDS, the final and most severe stage of HIV infection. This stage is characterized by severe damage to the immune system, making the body vulnerable to opportunistic infections.

list.title: Varied Symptom Onset:
list.snippet: While the acute phase is typically within 2-4 weeks, some individuals may not experience any symptoms during this time or even for years later.

list.title: Individual Differences:
list.snippet: The progression of HIV and the appearance of symptoms can vary significantly from person to person.

list.title: Testing is Key:
list.snippet: Due to the potential for asymptomatic periods, testing is the only reliable way to determine HIV status.

text_blocks.snippet: HIV symptoms can appear within 2 to 4 weeks after initial infection, often resembling the flu with symptoms like fever, headache, muscle aches, and swollen lymph nodes. However, some individuals may not experience any noticeable symptoms during this acute phase. In the absence of treatment, symptoms can remain mild or absent for years, but the virus continues to damage the immune system. Eventually, as the immune system weakens, more serious symptoms and opportunistic infections (AIDS) may develop.

list.title: Acute/Primary HIV Infection (2-4 weeks after infection):
list.snippet: Flu-like symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle aches, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and rash are common. Some individuals may not experience any symptoms at all during this stage.

list.title: Asymptomatic Period:
list.snippet: After the acute phase, many people experience a period with no noticeable symptoms, which can last for years. During this time, the virus continues to replicate and damage the immune system.

list.title: Late-stage HIV/AIDS:
list.snippet: As the immune system deteriorates, symptoms become more severe and can include persistent fever, weight loss, diarrhea, skin rashes, oral thrush, and opportunistic infections.
